subject: history
title: Abolition: Wilberforce & Equiano Adventure
welcome_lead: How did the British slave trade end? Meet William Wilberforce, Olaudah Equiano and the long fight for abolition. ✊
meta_desc: Abolition Adventure — a KS3 History walkthrough of how the British slave trade ended in 1807 and slavery in 1833.
final_note: You met key abolitionists and learned the key dates: 1807 (slave trade) and 1833 (slavery itself).

walkthroughs.body_html:
From the 1780s, more and more people in Britain spoke out against slavery.

Quakers, freed African writers and Christian campaigners worked together. They called themselves abolitionists.

Their tools were petitions, pamphlets, sugar boycotts, and the famous image of an enslaved man asking 'Am I not a man and a brother?'. 📜

William Wilberforce, an MP, gave speeches in Parliament for nearly 20 years against the slave trade.

Olaudah Equiano had been kidnapped from Africa as a child. He bought his freedom, came to Britain and wrote a famous book about his life. It opened many people's eyes.

Thomas Clarkson travelled the country collecting evidence — including chains and instruments of torture from slave ships.

In 1807, after long campaigning, Parliament passed the Slave Trade Act. British ships could no longer carry enslaved Africans.

But slavery itself was still legal in the colonies. So the campaign continued. In 1833, Parliament finally abolished slavery across most of the British Empire.

Enslaved people were freed — but plantation owners, not the enslaved, were paid huge compensation. 💷

options: Britain faced post-war labour shortages; the 1948 British Nationality Act gave Commonwealth citizens UK residency rights and Caribbean migrants answered the call to rebuild.

Windrush migrants were illegal immigrants from outside the empire.
